title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Food & Agriculture
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: France expects EU sanctions on 14 December over Iran’s sabotage of supermarket refrigeration, as Iran-linked hackers turn to physical attacks
items.content_text: France’s foreign minister said on 17 November he expects EU foreign ministers to agree sanctions on 14 December against those behind October’s sabotage of supermarket refrigeration controllers, a day after EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas confirmed new Iran sanctions are being prepared. Paris blames the IRGC’s Shahid Kaveh unit for the attack on about 700 French sites, which French authorities say caused at least 15 fires, and has sought arrest warrants for three officers; Iran rejects the accusations. Health-ISAC warned on 16 November that settings were also changed at French blood-service sites. US and Israeli officials told the Wall Street Journal that Iran-linked hackers also sabotaged equipment at small Midwest water stations and aboard two tankers. For grocers, cold stores and food processors, a state-backed actor has shown it will spoil food stock by remote control (editorial assessment).

items.title: CISA and FBI warn of an ongoing threat to internet-connected refrigeration as European supermarket attacks reach at least 11 countries
items.content_text: On 5 November CISA and the FBI, with HHS, USDA and DOT, warned that hackers tampering with internet-connected refrigeration controllers pose an ongoing threat that also reaches cold-storage, healthcare, chemical and transport operations. After hundreds of French stores were hit in October, a second wave on 1–2 November reached about 11 European countries, forcing units into continuous heating or defrost. Sweden’s NCSC says Coop and ICA victims mainly ran older systems from one manufacturer with weak passwords. Belgium’s interior minister said on 12 November that evidence points to Iran, short of formal attribution; a pro-Russian claim is unverified. Exposed Danfoss StoreView instances fell from 3,004 to 708 by 5 November, and Sekoia says the second wave used a non-public flaw that renames the controller’s admin account. Any reachable controller is at risk today (editorial assessment).

items.title: USDA takes farmer payment, mapping and contracting systems offline after a security breach
items.content_text: A security incident at the US Department of Agriculture has knocked farm-facing systems offline for several days. An internal email from an FPAC Business Center IT official, reported by Nextgov/FCW on 19 November, said USDA’s security operations centre “uncovered a security incident” and that all database passwords were reset, causing outages. ABC News, citing a notice sent on 16 November, reported that GIS mapping, payment and contracting systems were shut down; Nextgov says tools for farmer safety-net payments and loan-status checks were disrupted. Under Secretary Richard Fordyce told reporters, per DTN, it was a “cyberthreat,” not a software update, and that most systems should be back by close of business on 20 November. The attacker, entry route and any data theft are undisclosed. Producers should expect payment delays and phishing that exploits them (editorial assessment).

items.title: The Pentagon still will not say whether August commissary freezer failures were a cyberattack, as Army investigators work with French police
items.content_text: Investigators are still treating late-August refrigeration failures at no fewer than six US military commissaries, the on-base grocery stores, as a suspected cyberattack, with no cause confirmed. Reuters reported on 29 October, citing unnamed officials, that refrigerators and freezers switched to defrost and warmed, spoiling food at bases including Fort Huachuca and Fort Irwin, and that US Cyber Command has joined Army and Air Force inquiries. Stars and Stripes reported on 4 November that the Army CID cyber field office is working with the Defense Criminal Investigative Service and with French law enforcement on the October attacks in France; the Pentagon still declines to say whether a cyberattack occurred or how many stores were hit. Nextgov/FCW sources suspect Iran-linked hackers; no agency has attributed it. The forced-defrost pattern matches France, but this remains unconfirmed (editorial assessment).

items.title: Attackers rooted unpatched Check Point gateways through PHP2Shell, planted backdoors and wiped a VMware host; the root flaw is now in KEV
items.content_text: Check Point Research said on 12 November that attackers exploited the PHP2Shell flaws on unpatched Check Point Mobile Access portals from 30 October, then used a local flaw (CVE-2026-123039) to become root. They planted backdoors, pivoted to a VMware ESXi host and ran a wiper. The first wave hit Israeli organizations, some destructively; a second wave from 2 November reached several countries without destruction. Attribution is unconfirmed (tooling resembles China-nexus UNC5221). CISA added the root flaw to KEV on 13 November. No OT victim is reported, but these firewalls often sit at the IT/OT boundary and ESXi often hosts HMIs and historians (editorial assessment).

items.title: Cyberattack on Brazil’s Santos port authority forces manual workarounds at Latin America’s busiest port
items.content_text: The Port of Santos authority, which runs Brazil’s largest port, lost its IT systems on 6 November and on 10 November confirmed a cyberattack. Access-control systems and digital tools for coordinating port operations went down, delaying vessel, truck and train procedures and forcing some checks, such as matching ship dimensions to berths, to be done by hand. The port’s protection level was raised to 2 of 3 on 8 November. By 16 November main internal systems were in final tests and about 70% of affected file backups were recovered; ship movements and landside access continued throughout. Brazil’s Federal Police are investigating; the attacker, entry route and any data theft are undisclosed. Santos is a major outlet for Brazilian agricultural exports such as sugar, soy and coffee, so food and ag shippers should confirm their forwarders’ manual fallbacks (editorial assessment).

items.title: PHP2Shell attacks rooted about two dozen Palo Alto firewalls, and Siemens, Schneider and ABB now list grid-control, DCS and RTU products, several with no fix
items.content_text: Palo Alto’s Unit 42 verified that a suspected China-nexus actor chained the PHP2Shell flaws (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) with Linux kernel bug CVE-2026-46300 to root about two dozen internet-exposed PAN-OS firewalls on 23–24 October and steal Active Directory credentials. Siemens (Spectrum Power, AMIS TS and, since 16 November, WTV676/WTV776 metering gateways), Schneider (a Foxboro DCS server) and ABB (Netcontrol RTUs, ASPECT gateways) now list affected products, several unfixed. None is reported exploited and no OT operator is named: treat it as an IT-to-OT boundary warning.

items.title: Dragos counts 1,266 ransomware attacks on industrial organizations in Q3, up 11%, and found no case of an operator touching a control system
items.content_text: Dragos said on 16 November that ransomware hit 1,266 industrial organizations between July and September 2026, up 11% on the second quarter, while the number of brands claiming industrial victims jumped from 70 to 99. Manufacturing took 69% of cases, followed by the ICS ecosystem of integrators, engineering firms and equipment makers (116) and transport and logistics (105); oil and gas logged 47. Qilin and The Gentlemen drove 29% of the total. Dragos saw no Q3 case of a ransomware operator manipulating a control system: production stopped because the IT, ERP and virtualization layers plants rely on went down, as when Fairlife reportedly halted all four of its US plants for about 11 days. Entry came through edge devices and enterprise applications exploited within days of disclosure, and through stolen VPN and firewall credentials. Check Point separately counted a record 1,063 claimed victims across all sectors in October.

items.title: DHS tells Congress Iran-backed hackers have stepped up attacks on US water, energy and transport since February, while officials rule out hacking in last week’s outages
items.content_text: In written testimony for a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on 18 November, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Iranian state-sponsored groups and pro-Iranian criminals have targeted US critical infrastructure since the conflict with Iran began in February, with transportation, healthcare, water, energy and financial services increasingly in their sights. He described the attacks so far as mostly localized, low-damage disruptions of poorly secured industrial control systems, but warned that weak systems and poor cyber hygiene could have devastating consequences. At the same hearing the Director of National Intelligence and DHS said they found no evidence that hackers caused last week’s Microsoft 365 outage, the nationwide FAA ground stop or other recent disruptions, which officials tie to software defects and upgrade failures. Separately, AttackIQ research released on 17 November describes Iranian groups handing network access to one another, with long-running espionage access later passed to teams pursuing destructive goals, sometimes disguised as ransomware or hacktivism, often reaching targets through contractors and suppliers. For OT owners, the official US view now matches France’s: Iran is going after the weakest exposed controllers.

items.title: Bloomberg: Russia-aligned hacktivists have tampered with exposed controls since 2024, including at a Los Angeles-area meatpacker and two Spanish wineries
items.content_text: Bloomberg News published a review on 27 October of a loose network of hackers sympathetic to Russia that it says has carried out hundreds of attacks on water treatment plants, factories, dams and other sensitive sites in countries seen as hostile to Russia. The cases date from 2024 to this summer, and two touch food directly. Bloomberg reports that heating and ventilation systems at two Spanish wineries sent temperatures spiking in production and storage areas, and, according to Meduza’s summary of the paywalled article, that a meatpacking plant near Los Angeles had its refrigeration shut off in 2024, spoiling meat, followed by an ammonia leak that forced an evacuation. Who carried out or confirmed those food cases is not stated. The strongest confirmed case in the review is a water one: Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service attributed the December 2024 attack on the Tureby Alkestrup waterworks, which burst pipes and cut water to about 50 households for seven hours and about 450 for one hour, to the pro-Russian group Z-Pentest. The review covers groups including CARR and Z-Pentest; their own claims of further attacks are not independently verified. Editorial assessment: these attacks need no malware, only a remotely reachable controller with a weak password, which makes exposed refrigeration, HVAC and ammonia-plant controls in food facilities an easy target.

items.title: Hackers probe 14 newly disclosed flaws in end-of-life Copeland XWEB EVO refrigeration controllers, five of which will never be fixed
items.content_text: VulnCheck has disclosed 14 vulnerabilities in Copeland’s XWEB EVO, the Dixell supervisory system that runs supermarket and cold-storage refrigeration, each of which gave its researcher root on test units. Nine affect only firmware built before a 2021 rewrite and include unauthenticated command execution and a hard-coded admin password. The other five reach the latest firmware: the daily admin password is derived from the device’s MAC address and the date, and the MAC address is visible without logging in, so an attacker can compute the password, turn on SSH and log in as root. VulnCheck’s sensors saw exploitation attempts against two older-firmware flaws within two hours of the 12 November CVE publication; it calls the sources opportunistic scanners, not the state campaign in France. Copeland ended XWEB EVO support on 16 March 2026 and will not fix the five current-firmware flaws; nearly 2,000 units are reachable from the internet. CyberScoop adds that XBOW honeypots posing as these controllers drew hundreds of requests and login attempts within a day, and someone changed the temperature on one simulated freezer.

items.title: Six unpatched pre-login flaws in Danfoss AK-SM 800A refrigeration controllers prompt Belgian, German and Irish warnings to pull them off the internet
items.content_text: Amsterdam consultancy Midnight Blue has disclosed six stack buffer overflows in Danfoss AK-SM 800A system managers, the store-level controllers that run supermarket and cold-storage refrigeration, that allow remote code execution without logging in; one works even with “strict” session control turned on. All firmware up to 5.3.2 is affected and CVEs are still pending. The BSI says the 5.4.0 package released this month is not affected, but Midnight Blue says 5.4.0 predates its research and does not fix these bugs, so treat 5.4.0 as unconfirmed until Danfoss says otherwise. The researchers say an attacker could plant code that survives a factory reset or firmware update, or brick units, because the device does not appear to use secure boot; that is a stated possibility, not a demonstrated one. Belgium’s CCB and Germany’s BSI (13 November) and Ireland’s NCSC have all told operators that firmware updates, password changes and strict mode are not enough for internet-exposed units. Danfoss had published no advisory or fix date as of 16 November. No exploitation of these six flaws is reported.

items.title: A vCenter authentication bypass was exploited as a zero-day for two months before Broadcom’s 19 November patch; vCenter 7.0 gets no fix
items.content_text: Broadcom patched CVE-2026-123890 on 19 November, a critical flaw in vCenter’s directory service that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker obtain an administrator session. Google’s Mandiant, which reported the bug, says a suspected China-linked espionage group it tracks as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221, also called Warp Panda) exploited it for more than two months beforehand. In the incidents Mandiant investigated, the group got in through a BeyondTrust Remote Support flaw, moved to Linux appliances, attacked vCenter in early September with a custom tool called Bonesaw, stole SAML signing material and the vCenter master key, created an SSO admin account, forged tokens and moved on to ESXi hosts. Fixes are in vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m; end-of-life vCenter 7.0 has no public patch. No victims or sectors are named. Many plants run HMIs, historians and engineering workstations as virtual machines, so whoever controls vCenter controls those hosts (editorial assessment).
tags: Active exploitation — VMware vCenter authentication bypass CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS 9.8) exploited as a zero-day for more than two months by a suspected China-linked group, per Mandiant; Broadcom fix released 19 Nov 2026; no public fix for vCenter 7.0

items.title: Attackers root clustered Cisco Expressway gateways soon after a public exploit, and CISA adds the flaw to KEV
items.content_text: Security firm F6 says attackers exploited CVE-2026-76466, a critical flaw in clustered Cisco Expressway Core and Edge deployments, shortly after proof-of-concept code appeared on GitHub. They broke into two internet-facing Expressway nodes at an unnamed Russian organization, moved to two more cluster nodes inside the network, and gained root. From there they ran Python scripts, which F6 says show signs of AI-assisted writing, to scan for SMB shares, SQL Server and WinRM hosts and to search GitLab for credentials. CISA added the flaw to its KEV catalog on 20 November alongside the vCenter zero-day. Cisco disclosed and fixed it on 21 October; there is no workaround. No OT victim is reported, but Expressway is a perimeter gateway that often bridges outside callers into internal networks, so an exposed, unpatched cluster is a foothold close to plant-side systems (editorial assessment).

items.title: N-able ships Hotfix 3 for 17 more N-central flaws after attackers planted miners on servers already running Hotfix 2
items.content_text: N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3 on 16 November, which it calls a critical security update. It fixes 17 new CVEs, including authentication bypasses, missing authorization checks, path traversal leading to code execution and a syslog injection that runs commands as root, and it removes the Legacy API option that the actively exploited 4EverAble2Shell chain depends on. On-premises servers need the upgrade now; hosted servers update automatically, but every customer must also upgrade Agents and Probes, which N-able warns can otherwise be impersonated. The fix follows Huntback’s 13 November finding of cryptocurrency miners on 21 N-central servers, 19 of them on Hotfix 2. Remote control and Intune integration stay blocked for now. Separately, N-able said on 20 November that attackers reached a server in its hosted Mail Assure and SpamExperts email-filtering cloud, forcing it to take the management portal and APIs offline; it says mail flow continued, it has found no access to customer data, and the breach is unrelated to N-central. Many integrators manage plant-side Windows hosts through RMM tools, and a miner today can be a hands-on intruder tomorrow (editorial assessment).

items.title: Java4Shell exploitation attempts begin, and Siemens tells customers to take Industrial Edge Management offline until patched
items.content_text: Probing for Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption bug in how OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later decode Base64 data, started within two days of its 17 November disclosure. GreyNoise counted more than 150 matching requests from five addresses by early 19 November and Previdian logged nine attempts from six addresses; none is confirmed to have succeeded. Exploitation needs a recent Intel or AMD x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI, and researchers at Calif showed unauthenticated code execution against default Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Keycloak setups, each with a tailored chain. For OT teams the key item is Siemens advisory SSA-272816: three Industrial Edge Management products are affected, fixes are in progress, and Siemens recommends taking those instances offline until they are patched. Cisco lists more than a dozen products with no fix yet, and Atlassian Data Center products are also unpatched.

items.title: CISA republishes Mitsubishi Electric’s ICONICS advisory: a CVSS 9.1 flaw and a shared unlock code, with no fix coming for MC Works64, GENESIS32 or BizViz
items.content_text: CISA republished Mitsubishi Electric’s ICONICS advisory 2026-006 (vendor date 15 October) as ICSA-26-300-02 on 27 October. It covers GENESIS 11.03 and earlier; GENESIS64, ICONICS Suite, Hyper Historian, AnalytiX, MobileHMI and IoTWorX 10.97.3 and earlier; and every version of MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz. The most serious flaw, CVE-2026-16438 (CVSS v3.1 9.1 in the advisory), is an incorrect privilege assignment that the advisory says allows arbitrary operations. CVE-2026-16436 (8.1) lets a remote attacker unlock the system with a challenge response that is fixed and the same for every user, CVE-2026-16437 (6.4) lets a local administrator tamper with the file that stores it, and the bundled libwebp flaw CVE-2023-4863 (CVSS v3.1 8.2 in the advisory) can run code if an administrator imports a crafted file. The fixes are GENESIS 11.04 and version 10.98 of the GENESIS64 family (10.97.3 already fixes the libwebp flaw). Mitsubishi plans no fix for MC Works64, GENESIS32 or BizViz and recommends replacing them with GENESIS64 or GENESIS; until then it advises swapping the challenge-response file for a blank one with write access locked down, letting only administrators log in and blocking remote logins from untrusted networks. No exploitation of ICONICS products is reported; the libwebp flaw has been in CISA’s KEV catalog since 13 September 2023 because of browser exploitation. Editorial assessment: GENESIS64 and Hyper Historian are used for HMI, historian and energy monitoring in many process plants, food and beverage among them, and older GENESIS32 installations tend to linger on line PCs.

items.title: GAO finds USDA and FDA fall short on cyber threat sharing and emergency exercises for the food and agriculture sector
items.content_text: GAO reported on 19 November that USDA and the FDA, the sector’s lead federal agencies, met most cyber-related requirements Congress set in the FY2021 National Defense Authorization Act but only partially met or missed five, mainly on threat-information sharing and emergency preparedness. Both agencies cited a lack of resources and staffing, and ABC News reports they have not run food-sector cyberattack response exercises since 2024. GAO made five recommendations: two to USDA’s Office of Homeland Security and three to the FDA’s Office of Coordinated Outbreak Response, covering information sharing with CISA, preparedness exercises and, for FDA, planning documents for cyber emergencies. HHS agreed; USDA disagreed with its two and asked GAO to remove or redirect them, and GAO kept them. GAO recalls the 2021 ransomware attack on a global meat processor that shut major slaughterhouses. Plan to run your own exercises (editorial assessment).

items.title: CISA’s 2030 strategy puts OT protection and consequence-based prioritisation at its centre, but creates no new rules
items.content_text: CISA released “CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail”, a four-year strategy, on 26 October. Under “Defend” it names protecting operational technology — modernising OT environments and improving asset visibility and anomaly detection — alongside supply-chain integrity, and the agency says it will favour risk-informed, consequence-based analysis of the most important assets over a broad all-hazards approach. CISA will begin reviewing its core services within 60 days, deliver an implementation plan within 180 days and report progress after a year. The strategy creates no new legal authorities or obligations for operators, and some analysts quoted in the coverage question whether the agency has the capacity to deliver it after staff reductions. Editorial assessment: food and agriculture is one of the 16 critical-infrastructure sectors, so food operators that use CISA’s free services should watch what the 60-day review keeps.
